claim: Songbirds and humans share the ability to adaptively modify their vocalizations based on sensory feedback.
source: Songbirds and humans share the ability to adaptively modify their vocalizations based on sensory feedback.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that establishes the shared capability between songbirds and humans, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Prior studies have focused primarily on the role that auditory feedback plays in shaping vocal output throughout life.
source: Prior studies have focused primarily on the role that auditory feedback plays in shaping vocal output throughout life.
evidence: This statement references the focus of prior research, implicitly citing the body of literature on auditory feedback in vocal learning.

claim: It is unclear how non-auditory information drives vocal plasticity.
source: In contrast, it is unclear how non-auditory information drives vocal plasticity.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge about non-auditory contributions to vocal plasticity.

claim: Somatosensory feedback (cutaneous electrical stimulation) can drive vocal learning in adult songbirds.
source: Here, we first used a reinforcement learning paradigm to establish that somatosensory feedback (cutaneous electrical stimulation) can drive vocal learning in adult songbirds.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A songbird basal ganglia thalamocortical pathway is critical to auditory vocal learning.
source: We then assessed the role of a songbird basal ganglia thalamocortical pathway critical to auditory vocal learning in this novel form of vocal plasticity.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about the AFP's role in auditory vocal learning.

claim: The basal ganglia thalamocortical pathway and its dopaminergic inputs are necessary for non-auditory vocal learning.
source: We found that both this circuit and its dopaminergic inputs are necessary for non-auditory vocal learning, demonstrating that this pathway is critical for guiding adaptive vocal changes based on both auditory and somatosensory signals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by lesion experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The basal ganglia thalamocortical pathway is critical for guiding adaptive vocal changes based on both auditory and somatosensory signals.
source: We found that both this circuit and its dopaminergic inputs are necessary for non-auditory vocal learning, demonstrating that this pathway is critical for guiding adaptive vocal changes based on both auditory and somatosensory signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the pathway's necessity for both types of learning.

claim: The ability of this circuit to use both auditory and somatosensory information to guide vocal learning may reflect a general principle for the neural systems that support vocal plasticity across species.
source: The ability of this circuit to use both auditory and somatosensory information to guide vocal learning may reflect a general principle for the neural systems that support vocal plasticity across species.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Human speech is a prime example of a sensory-guided behavior.
source: Human speech is a prime example of a sensory-guided behavior, and humans are among the few species that use auditory feedback from their own vocalizations to compensate for perceived errors in vocal output (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Doupe and Kuhl, 1999.

claim: Humans are among the few species that use auditory feedback from their own vocalizations to compensate for perceived errors in vocal output.
source: Human speech is a prime example of a sensory-guided behavior, and humans are among the few species that use auditory feedback from their own vocalizations to compensate for perceived errors in vocal output (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Doupe and Kuhl, 1999.

claim: Loss of hearing impairs both speech development and vocal production in adulthood.
source: This reliance on sensory feedback for speech production is lifelong: loss of hearing impairs both speech development and vocal production in adulthood, and adult speakers rely heavily on auditory signals to calibrate their vocal acoustics (Oller and Eilers, 1988; Cowie and Douglas-Cowie, 1983; Stoel-Gammon and Otomo, 1986; Houde and Jordan, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations (Oller and Eilers, 1988; Cowie and Douglas-Cowie, 1983; Stoel-Gammon and Otomo, 1986).

claim: Adult speakers rely heavily on auditory signals to calibrate their vocal acoustics.
source: This reliance on sensory feedback for speech production is lifelong: loss of hearing impairs both speech development and vocal production in adulthood, and adult speakers rely heavily on auditory signals to calibrate their vocal acoustics (Oller and Eilers, 1988; Cowie and Douglas-Cowie, 1983; Stoel-Gammon and Otomo, 1986; Houde and Jordan, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Houde and Jordan, 1998.

claim: Studies of the neurobiology of speech have focused on the specialized neural pathways that process auditory feedback.
source: Accordingly, studies of the neurobiology of speech have focused on the specialized neural pathways that process auditory feeback (Jarvis, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jarvis, 2019.

claim: It is unclear whether the brain uses non-auditory sensory input to modulate the acoustics of vocal production.
source: In contrast, it is unclear whether the brain uses non-auditory sensory input to modulate the acoustics of vocal production, although studies demonstrating that humans use non-auditory (somatosensory) signals to calibrate jaw movements suggest that this might be the case (Nasir and Ostry, 2008; Tremblay et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge while referencing studies that suggest a possibility.

claim: Humans use non-auditory (somatosensory) signals to calibrate jaw movements.
source: In contrast, it is unclear whether the brain uses non-auditory sensory input to modulate the acoustics of vocal production, although studies demonstrating that humans use non-auditory (somatosensory) signals to calibrate jaw movements suggest that this might be the case (Nasir and Ostry, 2008; Tremblay et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nasir and Ostry, 2008; Tremblay et al., 2003.

claim: Songbirds rely on auditory signals to precisely calibrate their vocal output throughout life.
source: Like humans, songbirds rely on auditory signals to precisely calibrate their vocal output throughout life (Sober and Brainard, 2009; Kuebrich and Sober, 2015; Konishi, 1965; Nordeen and Nordeen, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations (Sober and Brainard, 2009; Kuebrich and Sober, 2015; Konishi, 1965; Nordeen and Nordeen, 1992).

claim: Songbirds have evolved specialized neural pathways for vocal learning.
source: Also similar to humans, songbirds have evolved specialized neural pathways for vocal learning, allowing the precise interrogation of the brain mechanisms of song plasticity (Jarvis, 2019; Brainard and Doupe, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jarvis, 2019; Brainard and Doupe, 2002.

claim: Prior research on the songbird vocal learning network has focused almost exclusively on the role of auditory feedback.
source: However, prior research on this brain network has focused almost exclusively on the role of auditory feedback, although recent work has shown the importance of visual cues (light) in shaping vocalizations (Veit et al., 2021; Zai et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement references the focus of prior research and cites recent work on visual cues.

claim: Recent work has shown the importance of visual cues (light) in shaping vocalizations.
source: However, prior research on this brain network has focused almost exclusively on the role of auditory feedback, although recent work has shown the importance of visual cues (light) in shaping vocalizations (Veit et al., 2021; Zai et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Veit et al., 2021; Zai et al., 2020.

claim: Songbird brains have a basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuit, the anterior forebrain pathway (AFP), that is required for auditory-guided vocal learning but not vocal production.
source: Previous studies have revealed that songbird brains have a basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuit, the anterior forebrain pathway (AFP), that is required for auditory-guided vocal learning but not vocal production (Figure 1a; Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Nordeen and Nordeen, 1993; Mooney, 2009; Bottjer et al., 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and references Figure 1a showing the circuit.

claim: Lesions of LMAN prevent adult vocal plasticity in response to perturbations of auditory feedback.
source: For example, lesions of LMAN (the output nucleus of the AFP) prevent adult vocal plasticity in response to perturbations of auditory feedback (Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Ali et al., 2013; Morrison and Nottebohm, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brainard and Doupe, 2000; Ali et al., 2013; Morrison and Nottebohm, 1993.

claim: Lesions or manipulations of dopaminergic input into Area X impair adult vocal learning in response to the pitch-contingent delivery of aversive auditory stimuli (white noise bursts).
source: Also, lesions or manipulations of dopaminergic input into Area X (the basal ganglia nucleus of the AFP) impair adult vocal learning in response to the pitch-contingent delivery of aversive auditory stimuli (white noise bursts) (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Hisey et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2016; Hisey et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018.

claim: The songbird AFP receives anatomical projections from brain regions that process non-auditory sensory information.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that the songbird AFP receives anatomical projections from brain regions that process non-auditory sensory information (Paterson and Bottjer, 2017), and that Area X plays a crucial role in processing visual information to shape vocal output (Zai et al., 2020), yet it remains unclear whether and how the AFP processes somatosensory feedback to drive vocal learning, and whether dopaminergic input to the AFP is involved in non-auditory forms of learning.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Paterson and Bottjer, 2017.

claim: Area X plays a crucial role in processing visual information to shape vocal output.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that the songbird AFP receives anatomical projections from brain regions that process non-auditory sensory information (Paterson and Bottjer, 2017), and that Area X plays a crucial role in processing visual information to shape vocal output (Zai et al., 2020), yet it remains unclear whether and how the AFP processes somatosensory feedback to drive vocal learning, and whether dopaminergic input to the AFP is involved in non-auditory forms of learning.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zai et al., 2020.

claim: It remains unclear whether and how the AFP processes somatosensory feedback to drive vocal learning.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that the songbird AFP receives anatomical projections from brain regions that process non-auditory sensory information (Paterson and Bottjer, 2017), and that Area X plays a crucial role in processing visual information to shape vocal output (Zai et al., 2020), yet it remains unclear whether and how the AFP processes somatosensory feedback to drive vocal learning, and whether dopaminergic input to the AFP is involved in non-auditory forms of learning.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: It remains unclear whether dopaminergic input to the AFP is involved in non-auditory forms of learning.
source: Recent work has demonstrated that the songbird AFP receives anatomical projections from brain regions that process non-auditory sensory information (Paterson and Bottjer, 2017), and that Area X plays a crucial role in processing visual information to shape vocal output (Zai et al., 2020), yet it remains unclear whether and how the AFP processes somatosensory feedback to drive vocal learning, and whether dopaminergic input to the AFP is involved in non-auditory forms of learning.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Adult songbirds can adaptively modify specific elements of their song structure in response to somatosensory feedback.
source: We first tested whether adult songbirds can adaptively modify specific elements of their song structure in response to somatosensory feedback (Figure 1b, Experiment 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data and referenced in Figure 1b.

claim: Mild cutaneous electrical stimulation was used as non-auditory stimuli delivered during ongoing song performance.
source: We used non-auditory stimuli (mild cutaneous electrical stimulation), which we delivered during ongoing song performance, to differentially reinforce the acoustics (fundamental frequency, or 'pitch') of specific song elements, or 'syllables.'
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Brief playbacks of white noise are a well-established paradigm for driving changes in pitch in adult songbirds.
source: In separate experiments, we tested birds using auditory stimuli consisting of brief playbacks of white noise, a well-established paradigm for driving changes in pitch in adult songbirds (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Andalman and Fee, 2009; Tumer and Brainard, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2016; Andalman and Fee, 2009; Tumer and Brainard, 2007.

claim: LMAN is the output nucleus of the AFP.
source: We next assessed the neural circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory-driven vocal learning by determining the necessity of LMAN (the output nucleus of the AFP) for somatosensory learning (Figure 1b, Experiment 2).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the songbird brain.

claim: LMAN is necessary for somatosensory vocal learning.
source: We next assessed the neural circuit mechanisms underlying somatosensory-driven vocal learning by determining the necessity of LMAN (the output nucleus of the AFP) for somatosensory learning (Figure 1b, Experiment 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by lesion experiments.

claim: Dopaminergic input to Area X is necessary for non-auditory vocal learning.
source: Finally, we assessed the role of dopaminergic neural circuitry in somatosensory vocal learning by performing selective lesions of dopaminergic input to Area X (Figure 1b, Experiment 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by lesion experiments.

claim: Songbirds naturally produce many renditions of song every day, which consist of repeated patterns of unique vocal gestures called syllables.
source: Every day, songbirds naturally produce many renditions of song, which consist of repeated patterns of unique vocal gestures, called syllables (Figure 2b, top).
evidence: This describes natural songbird behavior, supported by established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 2b.

claim: There is rendition-to-rendition variability in the fundamental frequency (pitch) of song syllables.
source: For one 'target' syllable in each experimental subject, we quantified rendition-to-rendition variability in the fundamental frequency (which we refer to here as 'pitch') of each occurrence of this syllable on the final baseline day (Figure 2b, top).
evidence: This describes an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Cutaneous stimulation was triggered in real time (within 40 ms of syllable onset) when the pitch of the target syllable fell within a specified range.
source: To differentially reinforce the pitch of a target syllable, we determined a range of pitches within this baseline distribution (either all pitches above the 20th percentile or all pitches below the 80th percentile), and then triggered the delivery of cutaneous stimulation in real time (within 40 ms of syllable onset) when the pitch of the target syllable fell within this range (Figure 2b, bottom).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Birds could choose not to sing in order to avoid triggering cutaneous stimulation.
source: Note that the birds could choose not to sing in order to avoid triggering any cutaneous stimulation, and we carefully monitored animal subjects for any signs of distress (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes an aspect of the experimental design and animal welfare monitoring.

claim: In the example experiment, the bird gradually changed the pitch of the targeted syllable downward (the adaptive direction), such that cutaneous stimulation was triggered less frequently.
source: In this example experiment, the bird gradually changed the pitch of the targeted syllable downward (the adaptive direction), such that cutaneous stimulation was triggered less frequently (Figure 2c).
evidence: This describes the results from an example experiment shown in Figure 2c.

claim: In the example experiment, at the start of the first day of cutaneous stimulation training, 80% of syllable renditions resulted in cutaneous stimulation and 20% resulted in escapes.
source: In the example experiment, at the start of the first day of cutaneous stimulation training, 80% of syllable renditions resulted in cutaneous stimulation and 20% of syllable renditions resulted in escapes.
evidence: This describes quantitative results from the example experiment.

claim: On the third (final) day of cutaneous stimulation training in the example experiment, escapes occurred on over 60% of target syllable renditions.
source: On the third (final) day of cutaneous stimulation training, escapes occurred on over 60% of target syllable renditions and the entire distribution of pitches had changed significantly in the adaptive direction, indicating that a significant amount of vocal learning occurred in this example experiment (Figure 2d; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test to assess the difference between baseline and end of cutaneous stimulation training, p=1.1776e-12).
evidence: This describes quantitative results from the example experiment shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The entire distribution of pitches changed significantly in the adaptive direction by the end of cutaneous stimulation training in the example experiment (p=1.1776e-12).
source: On the third (final) day of cutaneous stimulation training, escapes occurred on over 60% of target syllable renditions and the entire distribution of pitches had changed significantly in the adaptive direction, indicating that a significant amount of vocal learning occurred in this example experiment (Figure 2d; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test to assess the difference between baseline and end of cutaneous stimulation training, p=1.1776e-12).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the example experiment, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: After 6 days of washout, there was no significant difference between the distribution of target syllable pitches at the end of washout compared to baseline (p=0.606) in the example experiment.
source: After 6 days of washout, there was no significant difference between the distribution of target syllable pitches at the end of washout compared to baseline (Figure 2d; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p=0.606).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the example experiment, shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Semitones provide a normalized measure of pitch change such that a one semitone change corresponds to a roughly 6% change in the absolute frequency of an acoustic signal.
source: Semitones provide a normalized measure of pitch change such that a one semitone change corresponds to a roughly 6% change in the absolute frequency of an acoustic signal (see Equation 1).
evidence: This is a definition of the measurement unit used in the study.

claim: The mean pitch (in semitones) of the target syllables showed a significant, adaptive change from baseline on days 2 and 3 of cutaneous stimulation training (Pboot < 0.0010, n = 13 experiments in 12 birds).
source: We found that the mean pitch (in semitones) of the target syllables showed a significant, adaptive change from baseline on days 2 and 3 of cutaneous stimulation training (Figure 2e; the probability of resampled mean pitch on cutaneous stimulation training days 2 and 3 lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010, limit due to resampling 104 times, n = 13 experiments in 12 birds, one bird underwent two cutaneous stimulation experiments; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary statistical finding from the study, shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Non-auditory feedback is sufficient to drive vocal learning in adult songbirds.
source: This demonstrates that non-auditory feedback is sufficient to drive vocal learning in adult songbirds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing adaptive pitch changes in response to cutaneous stimulation.

claim: In all individual experiments where an upward pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (upward) direction.
source: In all individual experiments where an upward pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (upward) direction, and in all experiments where a downwards pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (downward) direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This describes consistent results across all experiments, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: In all experiments where a downward pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (downward) direction.
source: In all individual experiments where an upward pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (upward) direction, and in all experiments where a downwards pitch change resulted in less frequent triggering of cutaneous stimulation, the birds changed their pitch in the adaptive (downward) direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This describes consistent results across all experiments, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The order of white noise training and cutaneous stimulation training was randomized for birds that underwent both training paradigms.
source: To account for the potential influence of multiple trainings in the same individual birds on magnitude of learning, we randomized the order of white noise training and cutaneous stimulation training for the birds that underwent both training paradigms.
evidence: This describes an aspect of the experimental design to control for order effects.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference between the magnitude of learning by the end of training in birds that did not undergo craniotomies compared with birds that received sham LMAN lesions for either white noise experiments (p=0.779) or cutaneous stimulation experiments (p=0.148).
source: Also, we found no statistically significant difference between the magnitude of learning by the end of training in birds that did not undergo craniotomies for LMAN, 6-OHDA, or sham lesions compared with the magnitude of learning in birds that received sham LMAN lesions for either white noise experiments (two-sample t-test, p=0.779) or cutaneous stimulation experiments (two-sample t-test, p=0.148).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing learning magnitudes across experimental groups.

claim: By the end of white noise training, the adaptive pitch change (in semitones) across all white noise experiments performed in unoperated birds was significantly greater than baseline (Pboot < 0.0010).
source: Consistent with prior studies (Ali et al., 2013; Hoffmann et al., 2016; Tumer and Brainard, 2007), by the end of white noise training, the adaptive pitch change (in semitones) across all white noise experiments performed in unoperated birds (birds that had wire electrodes surgically implanted but received no invasive brain procedures like sham operations) was significantly greater than baseline (zero) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a; the probability of resampled mean pitch on all three cutaneous stimulation training days lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result consistent with prior studies, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a.

claim: In birds that underwent sham operations, significant adaptive pitch changes were observed in response to white noise bursts (Pboot < 0.0010).
source: In the separate experimental group of birds that underwent sham operations, we also observed significant adaptive pitch changes in response to white noise bursts, as expected (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b; the probability of resampled mean pitch on all three cutaneous stimulation training days lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from sham-operated birds, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b.

claim: There was no systematic difference between learning magnitude during cutaneous stimulation training and learning magnitude during white noise training (p=0.313).
source: We found no systematic differences between learning magnitude during cutaneous stimulation training and the learning magnitude during white noise training (Figure 2f; paired t-test, p=0.313).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing learning magnitudes between two types of training, shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Non-auditory stimuli can drive vocal learning as effectively as auditory stimuli.
source: These results suggest that non-auditory stimuli can drive vocal learning as effectively as auditory stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of learning magnitudes between cutaneous stimulation and white noise training.

claim: The normalized catch trials did not differ significantly from 1 in every experiment (0.071 < p < 0.997), indicating that the pitch of catch trials was highly similar to trials where cutaneous stimulation was provided.
source: In every case, the normalized catch trials did not differ significantly from 1, indicating that the pitch of catch trials was highly similar to trials where cutaneous stimulation was provided (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a; t-test, 0.071 < p < 0.997 for each experiment; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from catch trial analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a.

claim: There was no significant difference between randomly selected baseline trials and normalized catch trials (p=0.339).
source: There was no significant difference between this dataset and the normalized catch trials (paired t-test, p=0.339).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing catch trials to baseline trials.

claim: The cutaneous stimulation on the scalp did not drive learning through an unexpected influence on brain activity in dorsal auditory areas of the pallium.
source: To ensure that the cutaneous stimulation on the scalp did not drive learning through an unexpected influence on brain activity in dorsal auditory areas of the pallium, we implanted the wire electrodes in the neck instead of the scalp in 7 out of 12 birds used in these experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment comparing scalp and neck electrode placements.

claim: The magnitude of vocal learning did not differ between birds with scalp electrodes and birds with neck electrodes on any day of training (0.679 < Pboot < 0.891).
source: The magnitude of vocal learning did not differ between the two groups of birds on any day of training (0.679 < Pboot < 0.891).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing learning magnitudes between electrode placement groups.

claim: There was no significant difference in the magnitude of learning between song collected between 10 AM and noon and song collected between 6 PM and 8 PM on any day of training (0.167 < Pboot < 0.951).
source: Also, we reanalyzed this dataset by measuring syllable pitch from syllables produced in the evening (6 PM to 8 PM) instead of in the morning, and we found no significant difference in the magnitude of learning between song collected between 10 AM and noon and song collected between 6 PM and 8 PM on any day of training (Figure 2—figure supplement 7, 0.167 < Pboot < 0.951 on all days of training; Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from reanalysis of the data at different times of day, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The gradual, adaptive pitch shift is driven by non-auditory cutaneous stimulation and not by other unintentional effects of the stimulation, the methodology of wire implantation, or the time window of song analysis.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the gradual, adaptive pitch shift is driven by non-auditory cutaneous stimulation and not by other unintentional effects of the stimulation, the methodology of wire implantation, or the time window of song analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple control analyses ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: LMAN lesions induced a significant reduction in pitch CV (p=0.002), while sham operations did not (p=0.911).
source: LMAN lesions induced a significant reduction in pitch CV, sham operations did not (paired t-tests, p=0.002, p=0.911, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the LMAN lesion experiments, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Prelesion learning magnitude during cutaneous stimulation training was significantly greater than baseline (Pboot < 0.0010).
source: Prelesion, songbirds adaptively changed the pitch of the target syllable away from baseline in response to non-auditory feedback (the probability of resampled mean pitch on each day of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010) (Figure 3d, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from prelesion experiments, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Postlesion, non-auditory vocal learning was abolished in LMAN-lesioned birds (0.297 < Pboot < 0.660 on the final 4 days of training, n = 6 birds).
source: Postlesion, non-auditory vocal learning was abolished in those same birds (the probability of resampled mean pitch on each of the final 4 days of training lesser than or equal to zero was 0.297 < Pboot < 0.660, where 0.025 < Pboot < 0.975 indicates no significant difference, n = 6 birds; one bird from this group did not undergo prelesion experimentation) (Figure 3d, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from postlesion experiments, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Learning magnitude prelesion was significantly greater compared to learning magnitude postlesion in LMAN-lesioned birds (Pboot < 0.007 on each of the final 4 days of training).
source: Learning magnitude prelesion was significantly greater compared to learning magnitude postlesion (Pboot < 0.007 on each of the final 4 days of training).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing pre- and postlesion learning magnitudes.

claim: Significant learning during cutaneous stimulation training was observed in both pre- and postsham-lesioned datasets (Pboot < 0.0010, n = 5 birds).
source: We observed significant learning during cutaneous stimulation training in both pre- and postsham-lesioned datasets (Figure 3e, for both presham and postsham datasets, the probability of resampled mean pitch on each day of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010, n = 5 birds; Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from sham-lesioned experiments, shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The learning magnitudes during cutaneous stimulation training did not significantly differ in pre- vs. postsham datasets (0.120 < Pboot < 0.524).
source: Also, the learning magnitudes during cutaneous stimulation training did not significantly differ in pre- vs. postsham datasets (the probability of resampled mean pitch of presham data on each day of training lesser than or equal to resampled mean pitch of postlesion data was 0.120 < Pboot < 0.524).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing pre- and postsham learning magnitudes.

claim: The lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) for LMAN-lesioned birds was significantly greater than that for sham-operated birds at the end of fixed threshold training (p=0.036, n = 5 birds in both groups).
source: The lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) for LMAN-lesioned birds was significantly greater than that for sham-operated birds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p=0.036, n = 5 birds in both groups).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing lesion effects between groups, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) for LMAN-lesioned birds at the end of staircase training was significantly greater than for sham-lesioned birds (p=0.004, n = 5 birds in both groups).
source: The lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) for LMAN-lesioned birds calculated at this time point was also significantly greater than for sham-lesioned birds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p=0.004, n = 5 birds in both groups).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing lesion effects between groups, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: LMAN is required for non-auditory vocal learning in adult songbirds.
source: These results show that LMAN is required for non-auditory vocal learning in adult songbirds, indicating that both auditory and non-auditory sensory feedback engage the AFP to drive adaptive changes to song.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LMAN lesion experiments showing abolished learning postlesion.

claim: Both auditory and non-auditory sensory feedback engage the AFP to drive adaptive changes to song.
source: These results show that LMAN is required for non-auditory vocal learning in adult songbirds, indicating that both auditory and non-auditory sensory feedback engage the AFP to drive adaptive changes to song.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that LMAN is required for both auditory and non-auditory vocal learning.

claim: Selective lesions of dopaminergic projections in Area X were performed via bilateral 6-OHDA injections.
source: Selective lesions of dopaminergic projections in Area X were performed via bilateral 6-OHDA injections in Area X (see 'Materials and methods'), and the effectiveness of the 6-OHDA injections at lesioning dopaminergic innervation in Area X was quantified (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology for dopamine lesions.

claim: 6-OHDA injections selectively lesion dopaminergic inputs to Area X without damaging non-dopaminergic cells.
source: This approach has previously been shown to selectively lesion dopaminergic inputs to Area X without damaging non-dopaminergic cells (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Saravanan et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2016; Saravanan et al., 2019.

claim: Neither dopamine lesions nor sham operations induced significant changes in pitch CV (p=0.397 and p=0.531, respectively).
source: Dopaminergic lesions in Area X did not induce a significant change in syllable CV (Figure 4b; paired t-test, p=0.397; Figure 4—source data 1). Sham operations also did not induce a significant change in syllable CV (Figure 4b; paired t-test, p=0.531).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the dopamine lesion experiments, shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The lesion-induced changes in syllable CV (post – pre) were not significantly different for 6-OHDA-lesioned birds than for sham-lesioned birds (p=0.054).
source: The lesion-induced changes in syllable CV (post – pre) were not significantly different for 6-OHDA-lesioned birds than for sham-lesioned birds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p=0.054).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing lesion effects on CV between groups, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The dopamine lesion methodology used spares about 50% of the dopaminergic input to Area X.
source: It is likely that the dopamine lesion methodology we used, which spares about 50% of the dopaminergic input to Area X Hoffmann et al., 2016, is insufficient to impair dopamine-mediated generation of syllable variability.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hoffmann et al., 2016.

claim: Prelesion, songbirds adaptively changed the pitch of the target syllable during cutaneous stimulation training (Pboot < 0.010 on the final 4 days).
source: Prelesion, songbirds adaptively changed the pitch of the target syllable during cutaneous stimulation training (the probability of resampled mean pitch on each of the final 4 days of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.010) (Figure 4c, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from prelesion experiments, shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Postlesion, 6-OHDA-lesioned birds were not able to adaptively change the pitch of the target syllable during cutaneous stimulation training (0.067 < Pboot < 0.553 on the first 4 days; Pboot < 0.0010 on the final day, n = 5 birds).
source: Postlesion, these same birds were not able to adaptively change the pitch of the target syllable during cutaneous stimulation training (the probability of resampled mean pitch on each of the first 4 days of training lesser than or equal to zero was 0.067 < Pboot < 0.553; the probability of resampled mean pitch on the final day of training greater than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010, n = 5 birds).
evidence: This is a statistical result from postlesion experiments.

claim: Learning magnitude prelesion was significantly greater compared to learning magnitude postlesion in 6-OHDA-lesioned birds (Pboot < 0.0010 on the final 3 days of training).
source: Learning magnitude prelesion was significantly greater compared to learning magnitude postlesion (the probability of resampled mean pitch from prelesion dataset on each of the final 3 days of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to resampled mean pitch from postlesion dataset was Pboot < 0.0010).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing pre- and postlesion learning magnitudes.

claim: Both pre- and postsham, songbirds displayed significant amounts of learning during cutaneous stimulation training (Pboot < 0.0010, n = 3 birds).
source: Both pre- and postsham, songbirds displayed significant amounts of learning during cutaneous stimulation training (Figure 4d; the probability of resampled mean pitch from the presham dataset on each day other than day 2 of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010; the probability of resampled mean pitch from the postsham dataset on each day of cutaneous stimulation training lesser than or equal to zero was Pboot < 0.0010, n = 3 birds; Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is a statistical result from sham-lesioned experiments, shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The learning magnitudes during cutaneous stimulation training did not significantly differ pre- vs. postsham in dopamine lesion experiments (0.653 < Pboot < 0.931).
source: Also, the learning magnitudes during cutaneous stimulation training did not significantly differ pre- vs. postsham (the probability of resampled mean pitch of presham data on each day of training lesser than or equal to resampled mean pitch of postlesion data was 0.653 < Pboot < 0.931).
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing pre- and postsham learning magnitudes.

claim: Dopaminergic input to Area X is required for adaptive changes in vocal output in response to non-auditory signals.
source: These results demonstrate that dopaminergic input to Area X is required for adaptive changes in vocal output in response to non-auditory signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dopamine lesion experiments showing abolished learning postlesion.

claim: Adult vocal learning is not solely dependent on auditory feedback.
source: These results show that adult vocal learning is not solely dependent on auditory feedback, and that the songbird AFP is not specialized just for processing auditory feedback for vocal learning, as has previously been hypothesized (Murdoch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that non-auditory feedback can drive vocal learning.

claim: The songbird AFP is not specialized just for processing auditory feedback for vocal learning.
source: These results show that adult vocal learning is not solely dependent on auditory feedback, and that the songbird AFP is not specialized just for processing auditory feedback for vocal learning, as has previously been hypothesized (Murdoch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that the AFP is required for non-auditory vocal learning, contradicting a previous hypothesis.

claim: The AFP processes auditory feedback as well as non-auditory feedback to drive vocal learning.
source: Instead, these results, in conjunction with prior work using visual cues to drive changes in vocal output (Zai et al., 2020), indicate that the AFP processes auditory feedback as well as non-auditory feedback to drive vocal learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings and prior work on visual cues.

claim: The AFP processes somatosensory information to guide vocal learning.
source: Our results further show that the AFP processes somatosensory information to guide vocal learning, and that dopaminergic neural circuitry is necessary for non-auditory learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Dopaminergic neural circuitry is necessary for non-auditory learning.
source: Our results further show that the AFP processes somatosensory information to guide vocal learning, and that dopaminergic neural circuitry is necessary for non-auditory learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dopamine lesion experiments.

claim: Songbird vocal muscles use somatosensory feedback to compensate for experimentally induced changes in respiratory pressure during song performance.
source: Prior work has shown that songbird vocal muscles use somatosensory feedback to compensate for experimentally induced changes in respiratory pressure during song performance (Suthers et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Suthers et al., 2002.

claim: The AFP could play a role in processing somatosensory information from vocal muscles to guide song performance.
source: The result that the AFP underlies vocal learning driven by somatosensory signals (cutaneous stimulation) suggests that it could play a role in processing somatosensory information from vocal muscles to guide song performance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of the AFP based on the current findings.

claim: The AFP can integrate sensory information from a wide variety of sources of sensory feedback, even those not directly produced by vocalizations.
source: Also, the fact that mild cutaneous stimulation is different than the direct proprioceptive feedback from vocal muscles or vocal effectors, yet the AFP still underlies vocal learning in response to cutaneous stimulation, suggests that the AFP can integrate sensory information from a wide variety of sources of sensory feedback, even those not directly produced by vocalizations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that the AFP processes cutaneous stimulation, which is not directly related to vocal production.

claim: Songbird ventral pallidum (VP) receives input from auditory cortical areas, encodes auditory feedback information, and projects to VTA.
source: For example, recent work has demonstrated that songbird ventral pallidum (VP) receives input from auditory cortical areas, encodes auditory feedback information, and projects to VTA (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: The VP-VTA pathway represents a likely pathway by which sensory information from white noise bursts could influence neural activity in VTA, which could then drive changes in the AFP that promote song learning.
source: This represents a likely pathway by which sensory information from white noise bursts could influence neural activity in VTA, which could then drive changes in the AFP that promote song learning.
evidence: This is an inference about the neural pathway based on the cited work.

claim: Comparatively less is known about the pathways in the songbird brain that might carry sensory information from cutaneous stimulation to the AFP.
source: Comparatively less is known about the pathways in the songbird brain that might carry sensory information from cutaneous stimulation to the AFP.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Pathways for non-auditory information ultimately project to the VTA, where this information could be encoded and transmitted to the AFP to drive learning.
source: The results showing that dopaminergic input to Area X (which originates in the VTA) is necessary for non-auditory vocal learning suggest that pathways for non-auditory information ultimately project to the VTA, where this information could be encoded and transmitted to the AFP to drive learning.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about neural pathways based on the dopamine lesion results.

claim: Following dopamine depletions in Area X, songbirds displayed a small but significant anti-adaptive change in syllable pitch.
source: Following dopamine depletions in Area X, songbirds displayed a small but significant anti-adaptive change in syllable pitch.
evidence: This is an observation from the dopamine lesion experiments.

claim: The anti-adaptive change finding should be treated with caution because two of the four postlesion experiments had to be stopped earlier than expected due to pandemic-related disruptions.
source: We believe this finding should be treated with caution because two of the four postlesion experiments in this dataset had to be stopped earlier than expected due to pandemic-related disruptions, and the extent to which the change in significance on day 5 might reflect this issue is unclear.
evidence: This is a cautionary note about interpreting the anti-adaptive change result.

claim: Juvenile songbirds that receive both auditory and visual feedback from live tutors display more accurate copying of tutor songs relative to juvenile songbirds that only receive auditory feedback from their tutors.
source: For example, juvenile songbirds that receive both auditory and visual feedback from live tutors display more accurate copying of tutor songs relative to juvenile songbirds that only receive auditory feedback from their tutors (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Visual displays from adult song tutors positively reinforce the acquisition of specific song elements in juvenile songbirds.
source: Also, visual displays from adult song tutors positively reinforce the acquisition of specific song elements in juvenile songbirds (West and King, 1988), further suggesting an important role for visual signals in social interactions during song learning.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to West and King, 1988.

claim: Cutaneous stimulation can drive adaptive vocal changes in adult songbirds with similar effectiveness as auditory feedback.
source: Our results that cutaneous stimulation can drive adaptive vocal changes in adult songbirds demonstrate that non-auditory signals, even in the absence of any social cues or other reinforcing sensory signals, can drive vocal learning with similar effectiveness as auditory feedback.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of learning magnitudes between cutaneous stimulation and auditory feedback.

claim: The AFP might play a role in processing non-auditory sensory information important to other social behaviors that involve vocal communication, such as courtship, territorial displays, and pair bonding.
source: Further, our work suggests that the AFP might play a role in processing non-auditory sensory information important to other social behaviors that involve vocal communication, such as courtship, territorial displays, and pair bonding.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: A key function of the songbird AFP circuitry is to encode auditory performance error: the evaluation of the match between the auditory feedback the songbirds receive and their internal goal for what their song should sound like.
source: It has been hypothesized that a key function of the songbird AFP circuitry is to encode auditory performance error: the evaluation of the match between the auditory feedback the songbirds receive and their internal goal for what their song should sound like (based on their stored memory of the tutor song template) (Sober and Brainard, 2009; Saravanan et al., 2019; Fee and Goldberg, 2011; Gadagkar et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement references a hypothesis from prior literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: It has been difficult to determine the extent to which distorted auditory feedback drives adaptive changes in vocal output due to the aversive nature of the stimulus as opposed to the stimulus being interpreted by the bird as an auditory performance error.
source: It has been difficult to determine the extent to which distorted auditory feedback drives adaptive changes in vocal output due to the aversive nature of the stimulus as opposed to the stimulus being interpreted by the bird as an auditory performance error.
evidence: This statement identifies a challenge in interpreting prior experimental results.

claim: White noise bursts can often cause song interruptions at first, suggesting that they are startling to the birds.
source: Also, white noise bursts can often cause song interruptions at first, suggesting that they are startling to the birds (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Tumer and Brainard, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2016; Tumer and Brainard, 2007.

claim: Distorted elements of song syllable segments played during song performance elicit a pattern of activity in dopaminergic neurons consistent with the encoding of performance error.
source: Other experiments have used distorted elements of song syllable segments played during song performance (distorted auditory feedback) and found that they elicit a pattern of activity in dopaminergic neurons consistent with the encoding of performance error (Gadagkar et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Gadagkar et al., 2016.

claim: When bursts of noise are provided in non-vocal contexts, such as when a songbird stands on a particular perch, they can positively reinforce place preference.
source: Importantly, when bursts of noise are provided in non-vocal contexts, such as when a songbird stands on a particular perch (not during song performance), they can positively reinforce place preference (Murdoch et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Murdoch et al., 2018.

claim: It is unclear whether white noise bursts drive learning because the white noise is registered by the birds as a performance error or because the white noise is generally aversive.
source: Thus, due to the various nuances in experimental methodology and the inherent difficulty in measuring the aversive nature of the auditory stimuli, it is unclear whether white noise bursts drive learning because the white noise is registered by the birds as a performance error or because the white noise is generally aversive.
evidence: This statement identifies an unresolved question in the field.

claim: Cutaneous stimulation (an explicit, external, aversive sensory stimulus) is sufficient to drive vocal learning.
source: Although the results of the experiments described here do not directly address this, they do show that cutaneous stimulation (an explicit, external, aversive sensory stimulus) is sufficient to drive vocal learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The AFP may encode more general information about whether vocal performance resulted in a 'good' or 'bad' outcome, and it may use this information to drive changes to future motor output.
source: That the AFP underlies non-auditory learning suggests that the AFP does not solely encode auditory performance error. Instead, the AFP may encode more general information about whether vocal performance resulted in a 'good' or 'bad' outcome, and it may use this information to drive changes to future motor output.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The numerous analogies between the specialized vocal learning neural circuits that have evolved in songbirds and in humans suggest that the findings may be relevant to understanding the neural circuit mechanisms underlying human speech.
source: The numerous analogies between the specialized vocal learning neural circuits that have evolved in songbirds and in humans suggest that our findings may be relevant to understanding the neural circuit mechanisms underlying human speech (Doupe and Kuhl, 1999; Jarvis, 2019; Brainard and Doupe, 2002; Brainard and Doupe, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations about songbird-human analogies.

claim: Human speech depends on both auditory and non-auditory sensory information to guide learning.
source: Human speech depends on both auditory and non-auditory sensory information to guide learning, yet very little is known about the neural mechanisms for non-auditory vocal learning (Goldstein et al., 2003; Locke and Snow, 2010; Kuhl, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Goldstein et al., 2003; Locke and Snow, 2010; Kuhl, 2007.

claim: Very little is known about the neural mechanisms for non-auditory vocal learning in humans.
source: Human speech depends on both auditory and non-auditory sensory information to guide learning, yet very little is known about the neural mechanisms for non-auditory vocal learning (Goldstein et al., 2003; Locke and Snow, 2010; Kuhl, 2007).
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge about human vocal learning.

claim: The analogous vocal circuitry in humans may also underlie non-auditory vocal learning.
source: Our findings show that specialized vocal learning circuitry in songbirds processes non-auditory information to drive vocal plasticity. We suggest that the analogous vocal circuitry in humans may also underlie non-auditory vocal learning.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about human vocal learning based on the songbird findings.

claim: This neural circuitry in humans may underlie the processing of multimodal sensory signals during social interactions that modulate speech learning.
source: This neural circuitry in humans may underlie the processing of multimodal sensory signals during social interactions that modulate speech learning (Goldstein et al., 2003; Locke and Snow, 2010; Kuhl, 2007), or the non-auditory, somatosensory feedback from vocal effectors during speech production (Tremblay et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about human vocal learning, supported by citations.

claim: This neural circuitry in humans may underlie the non-auditory, somatosensory feedback from vocal effectors during speech production.
source: This neural circuitry in humans may underlie the processing of multimodal sensory signals during social interactions that modulate speech learning (Goldstein et al., 2003; Locke and Snow, 2010; Kuhl, 2007), or the non-auditory, somatosensory feedback from vocal effectors during speech production (Tremblay et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about human vocal learning, supported by citation to Tremblay et al., 2003.

claim: All subjects were adult (>100 days old) male Bengalese finches (Lonchura striata var. domestica).
source: All subjects were adult (>100 days old) male Bengalese finches (Lonchura striata var. domestica).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: All procedures were approved by Emory University's Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol #201700359).
source: All procedures were approved by Emory University's Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol #201700359).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: All singing was undirected (in the absence of a female bird) throughout all experiments.
source: All singing was undirected (in the absence of a female bird) throughout all experiments.
evidence: This describes an aspect of the experimental conditions.

claim: The duration of cutaneous stimulation was set to 50 ms.
source: We set the duration of cutaneous stimulation to 50 ms, which was a long enough duration to overlap with a large portion of the targeted syllable, yet a short enough duration to avoid interfering with following song syllables.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the experimental methodology.

claim: The magnitude of electric current used for producing the cutaneous stimulation was typically set to 100–350 μA.
source: We typically set the magnitude of electric current used for producing the cutaneous stimulation to 100–350 μA, which is behaviorally salient (the first few instances of cutaneous stimulation interrupt song), yet subtle enough as to not produce any body movements or signs of distress.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the experimental methodology.

claim: Stimulations typically occurred within 20–30 ms of target syllable onset.
source: Stimulations typically occurred within 20–30 ms of target syllable onset.
evidence: This describes the timing of the experimental stimulation.

claim: Spontaneous pitch restoration back to baseline was consistently observed across all experiments during washout.
source: During washout, we consistently observed spontaneous pitch restoration back to baseline across all experiments, which is in congruence with results from numerous white noise learning experiments (Hoffmann et al., 2016; Andalman and Fee, 2009; Tumer and Brainard, 2007).
evidence: This describes a consistent observation across experiments, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The number of songs sung per day did not differ significantly pre- vs. postlesion in LMAN-lesioned birds (p=0.249).
source: The number of songs sung per day did not differ significantly pre- vs. postlesion (paired t-test, p=0.249).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the LMAN lesion experiments.

claim: LMAN lesions in adult songbirds produce a significant decrease in the trial-to-trial variability of song syllable pitch.
source: LMAN lesions in adult songbirds produce a significant decrease in the trial-to-trial variability of song syllable pitch (Kao et al., 2005; Kao and Brainard, 2006; Hampton et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kao et al., 2005; Kao and Brainard, 2006; Hampton et al., 2009.

claim: The distribution of OD ratios from LMAN-lesioned tissue was significantly less than the OD ratios from sham-lesioned tissue (p<0.0010).
source: The distribution of OD ratios from LMAN-lesioned tissue was significantly less than the OD ratios from sham-lesioned tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p<0.0010).
evidence: This is a statistical result from histological analysis, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: All of the LMAN-lesioned birds had 80–100% of LMAN lesioned in both hemispheres.
source: We found that all of the LMAN-lesioned birds had 80–100% of LMAN lesioned in both hemispheres.
evidence: This describes the extent of LMAN lesions in the experimental subjects.

claim: The number of songs sung per day did not differ significantly pre- vs. postlesion in 6-OHDA-lesioned birds (p=0.290).
source: The number of songs sung per day did not differ significantly pre- vs. postlesion (paired t-test, p=0.290).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the dopamine lesion experiments.

claim: The distribution of all OD ratios from all of the 6-OHDA-lesioned tissue was significantly lower than that of the brain tissue from sham-operated birds (p<0.001).
source: The distribution of all OD ratios from all of the 6-OHDA-lesioned tissue was significantly lower than that of the brain tissue from sham-operated birds (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from histological analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: There was not a significant correlation between lesion size and the lesion-induced change in learning magnitude in 6-OHDA-lesioned birds (R2 = 0.019, p=0.137).
source: There was not a significant correlation between lesion size and the lesion-induced change in learning magnitude (post – pre) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and b; R2 = 0.019, p=0.137).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.
